notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material for Esther 4 from the older commentaries, Enduring Word, Bible.org, GotQuestions, Spurgeon and The Gospel Coalition. I ran out of searches before reaching the Catholic, Orthodox, NET Bible and Bible Odyssey sites, so nothing below comes from them. I also didn't find anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.

The real split in these sources isn't between denominations. It's over whether Mordecai and Esther are shown as people of faith (the book never names God) or as Jews who had drifted from God. I've marked that debate where it comes up. The tradition labels are the site groupings you gave me; the pages themselves don't name a denomination.

---

**vv. 1–3: Mordecai's mourning**

- **v. 1, the signs of grief.** Tearing clothes, sackcloth and ashes each signalled deep grief, and both together signalled the deepest grief possible. The Pulpit Commentary adds that Persians understood the gesture too. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-4.html
- **v. 1, why mourn in public.** Gill thinks Mordecai cried aloud so the Jews in the city would be alarmed and ask why. He also notes that Jewish tradition (the Targums) said Mordecai learned of the plot supernaturally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-1.htm
- **v. 1, Mordecai stands firm.** Guzik notes that Mordecai's integrity caused the crisis, yet he wouldn't back down and grovel before Haman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/
- **v. 1, Greek text.** Clarke points out that in the Greek version Mordecai cries out that a people who have done no evil are about to be destroyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/4-1.html
- **v. 1, debate.** Ellicott notes that the grief here is described only by outward signs. Nothing is said about praying to God, unlike Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah in similar danger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-1.htm
- **v. 2, the sackcloth law.** Matthew Henry says the king didn't want to hear complaints, so sadness was kept out of court. Banning the signs of sorrow without being able to ban its causes was, he says, a joke. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_004.cfm
- **v. 2, a sermon point.** The Pulpit Commentary calls it selfish power: the tyrant causes the misery and then shuts it out of his sight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/esther/4.htm
- **v. 2, a possible protest.** Deffinbaugh wonders whether Mordecai was a Jewish leader. His public mourning may have been a cue to other Jews, or an official protest aimed at the king. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-esther-s-dilemma-and-decision-esther-41-17
- **v. 3, a religious fast.** The Pulpit Commentary says the Jews fasted as a religious act, with repentance and prayer. Their cry couldn't get through the palace walls, but it would reach the King of kings. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-4.html
- **v. 3, an appeal to God.** Coffman agrees: even though God isn't named, the mourning only makes sense as an appeal for God to step in. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/4-1.html
- **v. 3, Jews who stayed behind.** Henry suggests some who had stayed in exile, out of weak trust in God, may now have regretted not going home under Cyrus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_004.cfm
- **v. 3, the opposite view.** Deffinbaugh stresses that the text never mentions repentance or prayer. From that silence he concludes that these Jews, Esther and Mordecai included, weren't godly. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-esther-s-dilemma-and-decision-esther-41-17

**vv. 4–9: Esther learns of the decree**

- **v. 4, a sympathetic reading.** The Pulpit Commentary thinks Esther didn't yet know the cause and assumed it was something minor, so she sent clothes. Mordecai refused without saying why. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/esther/4.htm Guzik agrees she hadn't heard of the decree, shut away in the palace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/
- **v. 4, a critical reading.** Deffinbaugh notes she first tried to stop the mourning rather than find out its cause. He asks whether Mordecai had become an embarrassment or a danger to her. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-esther-s-dilemma-and-decision-esther-41-17
- **vv. 5–8, a risky exchange.** Deffinbaugh says these very public messages threatened to expose Esther's secret Jewish identity. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-esther-s-dilemma-and-decision-esther-41-17
- **v. 7, the inside story.** Keil and Delitzsch say this verse shows Mordecai knew the private deal between the king and Haman, not just the public decree. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-1.htm
- **v. 7, the money.** Guzik says naming the sum shows Mordecai knew greed partly drove the plot. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/
- **v. 8.** Guzik says Mordecai sent a copy of the decree and challenged Esther to plead for her people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/

**vv. 10–12: Esther hesitates**

- **v. 11, the law and the 30 days.** Guzik says entering uninvited could mean death. Not being called for a month shows a Persian queen's marriage wasn't close. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/
- **v. 11, the king's temper.** The Pulpit Commentary notes the king was moody and hadn't asked for Esther in 30 days despite his earlier devotion. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-4.html
- **v. 11, a gospel contrast.** The Pulpit Commentary contrasts the two kings: Esther had no invitation, but God invites the repentant. Like the prodigal son's father, He watches for them to come. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-4.html
- **vv. 9–12, debate.** Deffinbaugh reads Esther's reply as a plain "No," driven by her own safety. He finds her unlike Daniel's three friends, and warns readers not to rush to call her a hero. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-esther-s-dilemma-and-decision-esther-41-17

**vv. 13–14: Mordecai's reply**

- **v. 13, a warning, not a rebuke.** Keil and Delitzsch say Mordecai isn't accusing Esther of not caring. He's pointing out that her own life is in danger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-14.htm
- **v. 13, no safe option.** A commentary quoted in the Light of Israel commentary says death awaited her either way, so she had nothing to lose. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/4-13.html
- **v. 14, "relief from another place," the traditional reading.** Mordecai is confident God won't let His people be destroyed. Without naming God, he trusts His promises (Pulpit). Keil and Delitzsch add that God's promise guarantees the nation's survival. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-14.htm Guzik says Mordecai trusted God's faithfulness, not Esther's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/
- **v. 14, "you will perish."** Matthew Poole sees it as God's judgment on cowardice and self-seeking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-14.htm Guzik says the people's fate rested on God, but Esther's own fate depended on her faithfulness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/
- **v. 14, a side note.** The Pulpit Commentary infers that Esther wasn't her father's only child. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-14.htm
- **v. 14, "who knows…"** Gill says Mordecai believed God's providence had made her queen to save His people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/4-14.html Keil and Delitzsch read the Hebrew as a broken-off sentence meaning "perhaps": an urgent charge to use her position. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-14.htm
- **v. 14, the dissenting view.** Ellicott questions how strong Mordecai's faith was. A truly faithful Jew, he suggests, might have gone back to Judea, and the conversation never mentions turning to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-14.htm
- **v. 14, a different translation.** Deffinbaugh follows the Catholic scholar J. Wiebe, who reads "relief will arise from another place" as a question expecting "no": Esther is the only hope. On this view Mordecai isn't trusting God. Breneman's commentary, as quoted there, objects that this limits God. https://bible.org/seriespage/3-esther-s-dilemma-and-decision-esther-41-17
- **v. 14, applying it.**
  - Spurgeon (Baptist) applies the verse to nations, churches and individuals placed for a purpose. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/esthers-exaltation-or-who-knoweth/
  - The Gospel Coalition (Reformed) sermon calls it probably the book's most important verse and says believers are placed where they are. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/for-such-a-time-as-this-en/
  - Guzik applies it to believers today. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/
  - MacLaren applies it to missionary work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-14.htm
  - GotQuestions says believers too are placed "for such a time as this." https://www.gotquestions.org/for-such-a-time-as-this.html

**vv. 15–17: Esther decides**

- **v. 16, the fast.** Benson says prayer was the main thing, with fasting only an aid to it. Matthew Poole notes that part of a day counted as a day, so she could go in on the third day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-16.htm
- **v. 16, the length.** Gill, following the medieval Jewish scholar Aben Ezra, takes it as two full days and nights, until the third day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/4-16.html
- **v. 16, Esther's maids.** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown thinks her maids were probably Jewish or converts. Cambridge doubts Esther kept the strictest form of the fast, since she had to look well before the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-16.htm
- **v. 16, still no prayer named.** Clarke finds it strange that even here neither prayer nor God is mentioned. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/4-16.html
- **v. 16, "If I perish, I perish."**
  - Gill sees content surrender to God's will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-16.htm
  - The Geneva Bible notes say she risks her life and leaves the outcome to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/4-16.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls it heroism inspired by God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-4.html
  - Guzik links it to Matthew 10:28 and Philippians 1:21, and ties the fast to Matthew 17:21. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-4/
  - GotQuestions calls it the turning point of her trust in God. https://www.gotquestions.org/if-I-perish-I-perish.html
- **v. 17.** The Pulpit Commentary notes Mordecai was satisfied and kept the three-day fast Esther asked for. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-4.html
